Choline hydroxide based deep eutectic solvent for dissolving cellulose† Yinglin Zhong,ª,b Jingwei Wu,ª,b Hongliang Kangª and Ruigang Liu 🆔 *ª,b,c

New cellulose solvent based on choline hydroxide/urea (ChOH/Ur) deep eutectic solvent (DES) was developed. The ChOH/Ur DES has a promising solubility for cellulose compared to ChCl-based DESs. ChOH/Ur DES with ca. 11 wt% water can dissolve at least 9.5 wt% cellulose with the degree of polymerization (DP) of 926 within 30 min. Compared to the ionic liquids, the temperature window of ChOH/Ur is wide and close to room temperature. The ChOH/Ur DES also showed more tolerance to water than ionic liquid, which can save energy in preparation and usage. The physical and chemical properties of DES and cellulose solution were investigated. The ChOH/Ur DES system is a non-derivatizing solvent for cellulose. The preliminary rheological results suggest that the dynamics of cellulose solution in ChOH/Ur system is similar to that of salt-free polyelectrolyte solutions. The degradation of cellulose during the dissolution and storage of the cellulose solution is limited. After 7 days of storage at 40 °C, the DP of the regenerated cellulose remained at about 80% of the raw material. The ChOH/Ur is recyclable without the loss of solubility of cellulose. In conclusion, the ChOH/Ur DES system is a promising green solvent platform for preparing regenerated cellulose materials and could be used as a media for cellulose chemistry.

## Introduction Cellulose, composed of linear β-(1→4)-linked glucose repeating units, is one of the most abundant natural biopolymers on the Earth and produced up to a thousand billion tons each year *via* photosynthesis. With the increasing demand for environmentally friendly and biocompatible products,¹⁻⁵ cellulose is considered as an inexhaustible source and a promising candidate for bio-based chemicals and fuels.⁶⁻¹⁰ However, the chain stereoregularity and abundant hydroxyl groups in cellulose lead to the formation of a strong hydrogen bonding network *via* the inter- and intra-chain hydrogen bonds. Thus, cellulose cannot be melted or dissolved in common solvents, which limits the application of cellulose, and only about 0.2% cellulose is utilized, mostly in the form of paper, textile, etc. Thus, finding solvents to break the hydrogen bonds of cellulose is crucial for the production of regenerated cellulose

Cellulose solvents have been developed for more than a century. By now, it can be classified into derivatizing and direct (non-derivatizing) solvent systems. The viscose process for producing regenerated cellulose fibers and films is a classical derivative system, which is still prevalent. In the viscose process, cellulose reacts with CS2 to form cellulose xanthonate and is then dissolved in NaOH aqueous solution to produce regenerated cellulose materials.11 The use of CS2 and release of toxic by-products in the viscose process cause serious environmental pollution and viscose plants have been gradually closed since 1980s in developed countries. Therefore, researchers are devoted to finding direct solvents of cellulose. The represented systems include N,N-dimethylacetamide/lithium chloride (DMAc/LiCI),12-14 N-methylmorpholine-N-oxide (NMMO) mono-hydrate,15 ionic liquids (ILs),16,17 and NaOH/urea aqueous solvents.18 However, these cellulose solvents still possess many problems. For example, pre-treatments via solvent exchange or high temperature are needed before dissolving cellulose in DMAc/LiC.19 Imidazole-based ionic liquid has an outstanding solubility for cellulose but is expensive with high energy consumption.20 Alkali urea aqueous system needs to previously freeze the solvent at a temperature below -12 °C and can only dissolve cellulose with relatively low molecular weight (ca. DP < 600).21 Thus, as a low-cost green solvent system, deep eutectic solvents (DESs) have attracted increasing attention recently.

DES is a mixture of hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA, e.g., qua-ternary ammonium salts) and hydrogen bond donor (HBD, e.g., amines, amides, carboxylic acids, and polyols).22-25 The earliest DES was reported by Abbott, a mixture of choline chloride and urea.22 The melting point of DESs is much lower than either of the individual components, which is due to the increase in the entropy of the system via the hydrogen bonding association of HBD and HBA.26 In addition, the physical and chemical properties of DESs can be readily regulated owing to the numerous (>106) possible combinations between HBA and HBD. DESs also have the advantages of easy preparation, low vapour pressure, non-flammability, biocompatibility, and biodegradability, depending on the species that used.23,27,28 DES is a promising solvent system for various solutes and chemical reactions.25,29,30 Because of the hydrogen bonding interaction of HBD and HBA, DESs could be a potential solvent system to dissolve cellulose as ILs. Several works reported the dissolution of cellulose in DESs.31-38 However, these DESs show poor solubility of cellulose and are invaluable for producing regenerated cellulose materials. Therefore, recent works of DESs mainly focused on pre-treatment, separation, and conversion of biomass.39-42 Inspiringly, recent reports indicate that ZnCl2 based DESs have a sound solubility of cellulose and can be used to prepare regenerated cellulose materials under mild conditions.43,44

In this work, our purpose is to find an efficient, economi- cal, and environmentally friendly solvent for cellulose. After systematical research, we discovered a choline hydroxide/urea (ChOH/Ur) DES system as a sound direct solvent for cellulose. The degradation of cellulose during dissolution and regener- ation procedures is limited. The ChOH/Ur DES is prepared from widely used chemicals and can be used near room temp- erature, from 30–70 °C, which offers to save the system cost and energy. ChOH is primarily used to produce choline salts, a kind of food nutrient additive and safe enough to be used in baby food. ChOH itself is also widely used as the cleaning and degreasing agent in the metal industry. Urea is a biological metabolite and used as fertilizer. ChOH/Ur shows the advan- tages of high water tolerance and excellent recyclability. Our

results suggest that ChOH/Ur system is a promising cheap solvent for cellulose, which could be developed into a state-of- the-art environmentally friendly platform for preparing regen- erated cellulose materials and a medium for cellulose chemistry.

## Experimental ### Materials Choline chloride (ChCl; 99%, Adamas-Beta) was recrystallized from absolute ethanol and vacuum dried at 50 °C overnight before use. The concentration of choline hydroxide (ChOH, ~45 wt%, Acros) aqueous solution was determined by titration with 0.1 M HCl solution. Urea (99%), thiourea (99%), resorcinol (99%), acetic acid (99%), L-histidine (99%), serine (99%), KOH (≥85%), and imidazole (99%), supplied by local chemical suppliers, are analytical grade and used as received. Microcrystalline cellulose (MCC, Alfa Aesar) and cotton linter pulp (Shandong Yinying Co., Ltd, China) were vacuum dried overnight before use. The degree of polymerization (DP) of MCC (DP = 145) and cotton linter pulp (DP = 541 and DP = 926) was measured by intrinsic viscosity measurements in 0.5 M cupriethylenediamine (CED) at 25 °C.

## Preparation of DESs The ChCl-based DESs were prepared according to the literature. 30,38,45,46 Briefly, ChCl was mixed with HBDs in a specific ratio and then heated to 60–70 °C with stirring until a clear homogenous liquid was formed. In the preparation of ChOH-based DESs, ChOH aqueous solution with known concentration was condensed by vacuum rotary evaporation at 67 °C, during which the vacuum gradually reduced from 1 kPa to 0.2 kPa. The relatively mild conditions could prevent the decomposition of ChOH during the condensing procedure. Water content was calculated from the loss of mass. The condensed ChOH was then mixed with HBDs to form DESs, following the same procedure as above. The details of the preparation conditions are listed in Table 1.

# Solubility measurements and regeneration of cellulose The solubility of cellulose in DESs was checked using the high crystallinity of MCC. ChCl-based DESs need enough time to dissolve cellulose. Thus, the freshly prepared ChCl-based DESs were divided into several equal parts, and a certain amount of MCC was added. The content of MCC in each part of DESs cellulose was in the range of 0–3 wt% with an interval of 0.5 wt%. The mixtures were heated under stirring at 100 °C for 24 h, followed by solubility measurements. The solubility of cellulose in DESs was estimated as follows. The above-prepared cellulose/DES mixtures were sandwiched between glass slides and observed under a polarized microscope (POM, Olympus EP50). A dark field in the view indicates the complete dissolution of MCC. Each experiment was repeated twice and the average was taken as the result.

For ChOH-based DESs, MCC was added in batches, and solubility estimation was carried out in 30 min after each addition of MCC. If completely dissolved, continued adding MCC until the insoluble matter was observed and recorded the concentration. Regenerated cellulose samples were prepared by pouring the cellulose solution into a coagulation bath of water or ethanol to precipitate cellulose and collected by filtration. Then, the regenerated cellulose samples were washed thoroughly with deionized water and vacuum dried at 70 °C overnight.

Kamlet–Taft parameters measurement of DESs The Kamlet–Taft (KT) parameters of DESs were measured using the solvatochromic dyes of 4-nitroaniline (4NA), _N_,_N_-diethyl-4-nitroaniline (DENA), and Reichardt’s dye (RD). In detail, 2 mg dyes were separately dissolved in 4 mL ethanol. A certain amount of the dye solution was transferred into a vial, and the ethanol was evaporated at 40 °C for 12 h. Then, DESs (2.5 g) was added to the vial and stirred to dissolve the dye completely. UV-vis spectra in the range of 350–700 nm of the dyed DESs were measured on a UV-vis spectrophotometer (UH4150, Hitachi) at 25 °C in a quartz cell of 1.0 mm light-path length. The maximum absorbance of the UV-vis spectra was controlled in the range of 0.4–2 by adjusting the volume of the dye solution added in the vials. ## Measurements and instruments The thermal properties of DESs were investigated using differ-ential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and thermogravimetric ana-lysis (TGA). DSC measurements were carried out on a differen-tial scanning calorimeter (DSC Q2000, TA Instruments, USA). The DESs samples were first equilibrated at 20 °C. Then, a cooling-heating cycle program between 20 °C and -80 °C was run with a ramp of 10 °C min⁻¹. TGA measurements were per-formed on a thermogravimetric analyzer (Pyris 1 TGA, PerkinElmer, USA). The DESs samples were heated from room temperature to 400 °C at a heating rate of 10 °C min⁻¹ in a nitrogen atmosphere.

Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectra were recorded on a Bruker Tensor27 FTIR spectroscopy. Each spectrum was recorded in the range of 4000–400 cm⁻¹ at the resolution of 4 cm⁻¹ with the accumulation of 32 scans. KBr pellets were used for sample preparation.

Wide angle X-ray diffraction (WAXD) measurements were carried out on a PANalytical Empyrean diffractometer with the Cu(Kα) radiation source (λ = 1.54 Å). The diffractometer was operated at 40 kV and 40 mA at the scanning rate of 2° min⁻¹ in the range of 2θ of 5°-40°.

Rheological properties of cellulose solutions were measured using ARES-G2 Rheometer (TA Instrument, USA). Two cone-plate geometry sets, 20 mm of 1° angle cone and 40 mm of 2° angle cone, were used according to the concentration of the cellulose solutions. Steady shear and dynamic oscillatory shear experiments were carried out in the shear rate range of 0.01–100 s⁻¹ and frequency range of 0.1–100 rad s⁻¹, respectively. For the measurement in oscillation mode, a strain sweep from 0.1 to 30% with a fixed frequency of 1 rad s⁻¹ was performed to determine the linear viscoelastic regime before each frequency sweep. A strain of 5% was chosen to fall well into the linear viscoelastic regime for the frequency range of 0.1–100 rad s⁻¹ in the oscillatory shear measurements. The experimental temperature was set at 25 °C, 35 °C, 45 °C, and 55 °C. A thin layer of low-viscosity silicone oil was smeared at the edge surface of the sample to avoid the influence of water evaporation or absorption on the rheological properties of the solutions during measurement.

Stability of cellulose in ChOH/Ur solution The stability of cellulose in ChOH/Ur solution was estimated as follows. The degree of polymerization (DP) of cellulose was determined using Ubbelohde viscometer. Cotton linter pulp was dissolved in ChOH/Ur, stored for different days at 70 °C, and then regenerated with deionized water. The samples were vacuum dried before DP measurement. To eliminate the mechanical effect on DP, such as agitation and shear, the raw pulp was treated with the same procedure as those regenerated cellulose samples. The DP of cellulose samples was evaluated from intrinsic viscosity measurements in 0.5 M cupriethylenediamine (CED) at 25 °C using the relationship reported by Marx.50

## Results and discussion ### Solubility of cellulose in DESs The solubility of cellulose in DESs prepared from different pairs of HBAs and HBDs reported in the literature was first checked. The results are listed in Table 1. Unlike the relatively high solubility of cellulose in DESs reported in the literature, e.g., 8 wt% in ChCl/Ur,46 10 wt% in ChCl/Thio,46 6.1 wt% in ChCl/Res,45 and 2.48 wt% in ChCl/Im,38 we found that almost all the DESs show negligible solubility of cellulose. In our experiments, crowding crystalline particles were clearly observed under a polarizing microscope even when the concentration of MCC was less than 0.5 wt% (Table S1, ESI†). The deviation from the literature could be attributed to the raw materials and the measuring method. In our measurements, no pre-treatment was performed on the raw materials, such as boiling or mercerizing, which could reduce the degree of crystallinity of MCC, and no third component was added into the ChCl-based DESs, such as water. It was reported that DES composed of ChCl and KOH can dissolve cellulose.51 However, we found that no DES can be formed and cellulose cannot be dissolved in this mixture. Based on previous works14,52,53 and the results in the literature,27 the higher basicity the HBA has, the stronger the ability to weaken the inter- and intra-molecular hydrogen bonds of cellulose. Therefore, the chloride ion in choline chloride was substituted by the hydroxide ion. It should be noted that it is very difficult to completely remove water in ChOH aqueous solutions. Thus, ChOH aqueous solution was only condensed to 80 wt%. Different HBDs were added in it to form ChOH based DESs. We found that only ChOH/Ur system has a relatively higher solubility of cellulose among the ChOH based DESs prepared in the present work (Table 1). By comparing the components of the DES pairs of ChCl/Ur, ChOH/Ur, and ChOH/thiourea, it can be speculated that the hydroxide ion and the carbonyl groups of urea should be critical for breaking the hydrogen bond network of cellulose and stabilizing cellulose chains in the media to form a homogeneous cellulose solution.

It is noted that the dissolving temperature of cellulose in ILs is in the range of 80–110 °C, e.g., 80 °C in 1-allyl-3-methylimidazolium chloride and 90 °C in 1-ethyl-3-methylimidazolium acetate. 62 The temp-erature for dissolving cellulose in NMMO·H2O is above 80 °C. Besides MCC, the solubility of cellulose raw materials with a high DP, cotton linter pulp (DP = 926), was also checked. The solubility of the cotton linter pulp in ChOH/Ur aqueous system with a water content of 11.8 wt% is 9.63 wt% at 70 °C, which is similar to the solubility of MCC. In prin-ciple, the solubility of a polymer in solvents is thermo-dynamically determined, which is irrelevant to the molar mass. The dissolving rate of cellulose with high DP becomes slower since it is kinetically unfavourable in the dissolution of polymers with higher molar mass. The little difference in the solubility of cellulose samples with different DP should be attributed to the experimental errors. The ChOH/Ur aqueous solvent system has a higher solubility than that of low temp-erature NaOH/urea aqueous system, which has a solubility limit of cellulose with relative low DP. 18 The promising solubi-lity for cellulose with high molecular weight is very important for developing the process to produce regenerated cellulose materials with desired properties.

in the literature. 65,66 The β value of the solvent is generally used to evaluate the hydrogen bond acceptor ability, which is highly correlated with cellulose solubility. 67 Some solvents, such as ILs, with β > 0.8 can easily form hydrogen bonds with hydroxyl groups of cellulose and has good cellulose solubility. 68 The β value of ChOH/Ur is 1.88, which is much higher than the β value of other DESs (<0.6) (Table 2). The high hydrogen bond basicity offers an excellent solubility of cellulose in ChOH/Ur DES, while the other DESs having a low β value (<0.6) and weak hydrogen bond basicity cannot dissolve cellulose.

Comparing the KT parameters of ChCl/Ur and ChOH/Ur, the α values are close to each other, but the β values are quite different. It can be speculated that the anions of the DES HBA have less effect on the hydrogen acidity but have a strong effect on the hydrogen basicity of DES. Therefore, replacing the anion of the choline based DESs with high hydrogen bond acceptor ability is expected to improve the solubility of cellulose. It can also indicate that hydroxide ion has stronger hydrogen bond acceptor ability than chloride ion, which is in line with reality. To clarify the influence of the water content in ChOH/Ur on the solubility of cellulose, the KT parameters of ChOH/Ur with 30 wt% water (ChOH/Ur–30% H2O) were measured. The β value of ChOH/Ur–30% H2O dropped to 0.46, and the α value increased to 0.98 at 25 °C (Table 2). It is known that water has a low hydrogen bond basicity (β = 0.18) and a high hydrogen bond acidity (α = 1.17).69,70 The changes in KT parameters of ChOH/Ur with the addition of water in the system could be attributed to the strong interaction between water molecules and the OH- ions of ChOH/Ur and weaken the hydrogen bond basicity of the solvent. The presence of excess water molecules can compete with cellulose in the formation of hydrogen bonds, which leads to reducing the solubility of cellulose in ChOH/Ur DES. Molecular dynamic simulation and vibrational analysis of ChCl/Ur (1:2) indicated that there is a strong interaction between –NH2 of urea and chlorine anion where the system tends to maximize the number of hydrogen bonds to the anion,71,72 which could reduce the ability for the chlorine anion to break the hydrogen bonds of cellulose.

The KT parameters of CHOH-based DESs indicate that the HBD species also have a significant impact on the β value. ChOH/Res and ChOH/Im have the β value of 0.53 and 0.57, respectively (Table 2). The results suggest that HBD selection is another important factor to dissolve cellulose. That is different from pure ILs, of which β is dominated by anionic species.73 In the case of DESs, β is influenced by both the HBA anion and the HBD component, which could be attributed to the interactions between HBA and HBD in the formation of DESs. The formation of DESs via the establishment of hydrogen bonds between HBD and HBA results in a decrease in the capacity to engage in further hydrogen bond networks.74 In other words, strong hydrogen bonds between HBA and HBD will lead to a decrease in β value, which is unfavourable for dis-solving cellulose. That means cellulose and the HBD of DESs are somewhat in a competitive relationship. If the hydrogen bonding interaction between HBD and HBA of DES is stronger

than that between cellulose and HBA, the β value of the DESS and their solubility of cellulose would be lowered as the ChOH-based DESs other than ChOH/Ur in this work (Tables 1 and 2). In principle, a low α value and a high β value of the HBD itself is preferred in preparing DESs to dissolve cellulose, which seems to contradict the identity as "hydrogen bond donor". According to this speculation, DMSO, with α = 0.19, β = 0.73, could be a good candidate for HBD in preparing DES for dissolving cellulose. We found that the ChOH/DMSO (1:2) system could dissolve MCC at least 10 wt%. The details of the ChOH/DMSO system will be reported in our future work. Urea has been reported to promote the solubility of cellulose in alkali¹⁸,⁵³ and TBAH⁷⁵ aqueous solvent systems, in which urea helped to stabilize the isolated cellulose chains in the solution. In ChOH/Ur system, the ChOH and urea act as HBA and HBD, respectively, to form a DES via strong hydrogen bonding interactions. As a new DES, the structure of ChOH/Ur DES is still not fully understood. Speculated from the results of ChCl/Ur system,⁷¹,⁷² there is a strong interaction between -NH₂ of urea and anion of chlorine hydroxide, which forms moderate hydrogen bonds in the ChOH/Ur DES system. Therefore, the function of urea in ChOh/Ur system is different from that in the alkali and TBAH systems. More experimental and theoretical works are needed to clarify the mechanism of the dissolution of cellulose in ChOH/Ur system.

## Rheology of cellulose/ChOH/Ur solutions Steady and complex viscosity of cellulose/ChOH/Ur aqueous solutions with different cellulose concentrations at different temperatures were measured. The DP of the cellulose is 541 for all the rheological measurements. Fig. 4a shows the steady shear solution viscosity as a function of shear rate. The results indicate that the pure ChOH/Ur DES solvent shows a Newtonian behaviour. The cellulose/ChOH/Ur solutions show the typical shear-thinning behaviour at higher shear rates, and the onset of shear thinning shifts to a lower shear rate with the increase in cellulose concentration. The results are similar to those of cellulose/ionic liquid solutions.76,77

# Conclusions A systematic investigation has confirmed that almost all the ChCl-based DESs reported in the literature cannot dissolve cellulose. A new ChOH/Ur DES, with ChOH as the HBA and urea as HBD, was found with a sound solubility of cellulose. The ChOH/Ur system with ca. 11 wt% water can dissolve at least ~9.5 wt% cellulose with DP of 926 (cotton litter pulp). The maximum value of solubility was achieved at 70 °C within 30 min at the laboratory level. Our results also showed that the ChOH/Ur DES is tolerant to water. ChOH/Ur is a direct solvent system for cellulose, and no derivatizing reaction was found during the dissolution. Kamlet-Taft parameters of the EDSs were measured, and the results indicated that ChOH/Ur has a strong hydrogen bond basicity with the \u03b2 value of 1.88. The preliminary rheological results suggest that the dynamics of cellulose solution in ChOH/Ur system is similar to that of salt-free polyelectrolyte solutions. The degradation of cellulose during the dissolution and storage is limited. After the cellulose/ChOH/Ur solution was stored at 40 °C for 7 days, the DP of the regenerated cellulose remained about 80% of raw materials. The ChOH/Ur DES is recyclable without losing the solubility of cellulose. The ChOH/Ur DES is a promising solvent platform for preparing regenerated cellulose materials and may also be a media for cellulose chemistry.

The ChOH/Ur DES has a promising solubility for cellulose compared to ChCl-based DESs. ChOH/Ur DES with ca. 11 wt% water can dissolve at least 9.5 wt% cellulose with the degree of polymerization (DP) of 926 within 30 min. Compared to the ionic liquids, the temperature window of ChOH/Ur is wide and close to room temperature. The ChOH/Ur DES also showed more tolerance to water than ionic liquid, which can save energy in preparation and usage. The physical and chemical properties of DES and cellulose solution were investigated. The ChOH/Ur DES system is a non-derivatizing solvent for cellulose. The preliminary rheological results suggest that the dynamics of cellulose solution in ChOH/Ur system is similar to that of salt-free polyelectrolyte solutions. The degradation of cellulose during the dissolution and storage of the cellulose solution is limited. After 7 days of storage at 40 °C, the DP of the regenerated cellulose remained at about 80% of the raw material. The ChOH/Ur is recyclable without the loss of solubility of cellulose. In conclusion, the ChOH/Ur DES system is a promising green solvent platform for preparing regenerated cellulose materials and could be used as a media for cellulose chemistry. ## Introduction Cellulose, composed of linear β-(1→4)-linked glucose repeating units, is one of the most abundant natural biopolymers on the Earth and produced up to a thousand billion tons each year *via* photosynthesis. With the increasing demand for environmentally friendly and biocompatible products,¹⁻⁵ cellulose is considered as an inexhaustible source and a promising candidate for bio-based chemicals and fuels.⁶⁻¹⁰ However, the chain stereoregularity and abundant hydroxyl groups in cellulose lead to the formation of a strong hydrogen bonding network *via* the inter- and intra-chain hydrogen bonds. Thus, cellulose cannot be melted or dissolved in common solvents, which limits the application of cellulose, and only about 0.2% cellulose is utilized, mostly in the form of paper, textile, etc. Thus, finding solvents to break the hydrogen bonds of cellulose is crucial for the production of regenerated cellulose ᵃLaboratory of Polymer Physics and Chemistry, Beijing National Laboratory of Molecular Sciences, Institute of Chemistry, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100190, China. See DOI: 10.1039/ d1gc04130d materials and the modification of cellulose into functional materials. Cellulose solvents have been developed for more than a century. By now, it can be classified into derivatizing and direct (non-derivatizing) solvent systems. The viscose process for producing regenerated cellulose fibers and films is a classical derivative system, which is still prevalent. In the viscose process, cellulose reacts with CS2 to form cellulose xanthonate and is then dissolved in NaOH aqueous solution to produce regenerated cellulose materials.11 The use of CS2 and release of toxic by-products in the viscose process cause serious environmental pollution and viscose plants have been gradually closed since 1980s in developed countries. Therefore, researchers are devoted to finding direct solvents of cellulose. The represented systems include N,N-dimethylacetamide/lithium chloride (DMAc/LiCI),12-14 N-methylmorpholine-N-oxide (NMMO) mono-hydrate,15 ionic liquids (ILs),16,17 and NaOH/urea aqueous solvents.18 However, these cellulose solvents still possess many problems. For example, pre-treatments via solvent exchange or high temperature are needed before dissolving cellulose in DMAc/LiC.19 Imidazole-based ionic liquid has an outstanding solubility for cellulose but is expensive with high energy consumption.20 Alkali urea aqueous system needs to previously freeze the solvent at a temperature below -12 °C and can only dissolve cellulose with relatively low molecular weight (ca. DP < 600).21 Thus, as a low-cost green solvent system, deep eutectic solvents (DESs) have attracted increasing attention recently. 2464 | Green Chem., 2022, 24, 2464-2475 This journal is  The Royal Society of Chemistry 2022 Published on 14 February 2022. View Article Online Green Chemistry Paper DES is a mixture of hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA, e.g., qua-ternary ammonium salts) and hydrogen bond donor (HBD, e.g., amines, amides, carboxylic acids, and polyols).22-25 The earliest DES was reported by Abbott, a mixture of choline chloride and urea.22 The melting point of DESs is much lower than either of the individual components, which is due to the increase in the entropy of the system via the hydrogen bonding association of HBD and HBA.26 In addition, the physical and chemical properties of DESs can be readily regulated owing to the numerous (>106) possible combinations between HBA and HBD. DESs also have the advantages of easy preparation, low vapour pressure, non-flammability, biocompatibility, and biodegradability, depending on the species that used.23,27,28 DES is a promising solvent system for various solutes and chemical reactions.25,29,30 Because of the hydrogen bonding interaction of HBD and HBA, DESs could be a potential solvent system to dissolve cellulose as ILs. Several works reported the dissolution of cellulose in DESs.31-38 However, these DESs show poor solubility of cellulose and are invaluable for producing regenerated cellulose materials. Therefore, recent works of DESs mainly focused on pre-treatment, separation, and conversion of biomass.39-42 Inspiringly, recent reports indicate that ZnCl2 based DESs have a sound solubility of cellulose and can be used to prepare regenerated cellulose materials under mild conditions.43,44 In this work, our purpose is to find an efficient, economi- cal, and environmentally friendly solvent for cellulose. After systematical research, we discovered a choline hydroxide/urea (ChOH/Ur) DES system as a sound direct solvent for cellulose. The degradation of cellulose during dissolution and regener- ation procedures is limited. The ChOH/Ur DES is prepared from widely used chemicals and can be used near room temp- erature, from 30–70 °C, which offers to save the system cost and energy. ChOH is primarily used to produce choline salts, a kind of food nutrient additive and safe enough to be used in baby food. ChOH itself is also widely used as the cleaning and degreasing agent in the metal industry. Urea is a biological metabolite and used as fertilizer. ChOH/Ur shows the advan- tages of high water tolerance and excellent recyclability. Our results suggest that ChOH/Ur system is a promising cheap solvent for cellulose, which could be developed into a state-of- the-art environmentally friendly platform for preparing regen- erated cellulose materials and a medium for cellulose chemistry. ## Experimental ### Materials Choline chloride (ChCl; 99%, Adamas-Beta) was recrystallized from absolute ethanol and vacuum dried at 50 °C overnight before use. The concentration of choline hydroxide (ChOH, ~45 wt%, Acros) aqueous solution was determined by titration with 0.1 M HCl solution. Urea (99%), thiourea (99%), resorcinol (99%), acetic acid (99%), L-histidine (99%), serine (99%), KOH (≥85%), and imidazole (99%), supplied by local chemical suppliers, are analytical grade and used as received. Microcrystalline cellulose (MCC, Alfa Aesar) and cotton linter pulp (Shandong Yinying Co., Ltd, China) were vacuum dried overnight before use. The degree of polymerization (DP) of MCC (DP = 145) and cotton linter pulp (DP = 541 and DP = 926) was measured by intrinsic viscosity measurements in 0.5 M cupriethylenediamine (CED) at 25 °C. ## Preparation of DESs The ChCl-based DESs were prepared according to the literature. 30,38,45,46 Briefly, ChCl was mixed with HBDs in a specific ratio and then heated to 60–70 °C with stirring until a clear homogenous liquid was formed. In the preparation of ChOH-based DESs, ChOH aqueous solution with known concentration was condensed by vacuum rotary evaporation at 67 °C, during which the vacuum gradually reduced from 1 kPa to 0.2 kPa. The relatively mild conditions could prevent the decomposition of ChOH during the condensing procedure. Water content was calculated from the loss of mass. The condensed ChOH was then mixed with HBDs to form DESs, following the same procedure as above. The details of the preparation conditions are listed in Table 1. View Article Online Green Chemistry Paper ## Results and discussion ### Solubility of cellulose in DESs The solubility of cellulose in DESs prepared from different pairs of HBAs and HBDs reported in the literature was first checked. The results are listed in Table 1. Unlike the relatively high solubility of cellulose in DESs reported in the literature, e.g., 8 wt% in ChCl/Ur,46 10 wt% in ChCl/Thio,46 6.1 wt% in ChCl/Res,45 and 2.48 wt% in ChCl/Im,38 we found that almost all the DESs show negligible solubility of cellulose. In our experiments, crowding crystalline particles were clearly observed under a polarizing microscope even when the concentration of MCC was less than 0.5 wt% (Table S1, ESI†). The deviation from the literature could be attributed to the raw materials and the measuring method. In our measurements, no pre-treatment was performed on the raw materials, such as boiling or mercerizing, which could reduce the degree of crystallinity of MCC, and no third component was added into the ChCl-based DESs, such as water. It was reported that DES composed of ChCl and KOH can dissolve cellulose.51 However, we found that no DES can be formed and cellulose cannot be dissolved in this mixture. Based on previous works14,52,53 and the results in the literature,27 the higher basicity the HBA has, the stronger the ability to weaken the inter- and intra-molecular hydrogen bonds of cellulose. Therefore, the chloride ion in choline chloride was substituted by the hydroxide ion. It should be noted that it is very difficult to completely remove water in ChOH aqueous solutions. Thus, ChOH aqueous solution was only condensed to 80 wt%. Different HBDs were added in it to form ChOH based DESs. We found that only ChOH/Ur system has a relatively higher solubility of cellulose among the ChOH based DESs prepared in the present work (Table 1). By comparing the components of the DES pairs of ChCl/Ur, ChOH/Ur, and ChOH/thiourea, it can be speculated that the hydroxide ion and the carbonyl groups of urea should be critical for breaking the hydrogen bond network of cellulose and stabilizing cellulose chains in the media to form a homogeneous cellulose solution. It is reasonable that water molecules participate in the hydrogen bond formation inside the system. ⁵⁹ The interaction of water molecules and solvent system competing with that of cellulose molecules and solvent system results in reducing the solubility of cellulose. The results confirm that cellulose degradation in the ChOH/Ur DES system is limited, and the ChOH/Ur solvent system is promising for preparing high-performance regener- ated cellulose materials. # Conclusions A systematic investigation has confirmed that almost all the ChCl-based DESs reported in the literature cannot dissolve cellulose. A new ChOH/Ur DES, with ChOH as the HBA and urea as HBD, was found with a sound solubility of cellulose. The ChOH/Ur system with ca. 11 wt% water can dissolve at least ~9.5 wt% cellulose with DP of 926 (cotton litter pulp). The maximum value of solubility was achieved at 70 °C within 30 min at the laboratory level. Our results also showed that the ChOH/Ur DES is tolerant to water. ChOH/Ur is a direct solvent system for cellulose, and no derivatizing reaction was found during the dissolution. Kamlet-Taft parameters of the EDSs were measured, and the results indicated that ChOH/Ur has a strong hydrogen bond basicity with the \u03b2 value of 1.88. The preliminary rheological results suggest that the dynamics of cellulose solution in ChOH/Ur system is similar to that of salt-free polyelectrolyte solutions. The degradation of cellulose during the dissolution and storage is limited. After the cellulose/ChOH/Ur solution was stored at 40 °C for 7 days, the DP of the regenerated cellulose remained about 80% of raw materials. The ChOH/Ur DES is recyclable without losing the solubility of cellulose. The ChOH/Ur DES is a promising solvent platform for preparing regenerated cellulose materials and may also be a media for cellulose chemistry. ## Conflicts of interest There are no conflicts to declare. Compared to the ionic liquids, the temperature window of ChOH/Ur is wide and close to room temperature. The physical and chemical properties of DES and cellulose solution were investigated. The ChOH/Ur DES system is a non-derivatizing solvent for cellulose. In the viscose process, cellulose reacts with CS2 to form cellulose xanthonate and is then dissolved in NaOH aqueous solution to produce regenerated cellulose materials.11 The use of CS2 and release of toxic by-products in the viscose process cause serious environmental pollution and viscose plants have been gradually closed since 1980s in developed countries. DESs also have the advantages of easy preparation, low vapour pressure, non-flammability, biocompatibility, and biodegradability, depending on the species that used.23,27,28 DES is a promising solvent system for various solutes and chemical reactions.25,29,30 Because of the hydrogen bonding interaction of HBD and HBA, DESs could be a potential solvent system to dissolve cellulose as ILs. Several works reported the dissolution of cellulose in DESs.31-38 However, these DESs show poor solubility of cellulose and are invaluable for producing regenerated cellulose materials. Therefore, recent works of DESs mainly focused on pre-treatment, separation, and conversion of biomass.39-42 Inspiringly, recent reports indicate that ZnCl2 based DESs have a sound solubility of cellulose and can be used to prepare regenerated cellulose materials under mild conditions.43,44 In this work, our purpose is to find an efficient, economi- cal, and environmentally friendly solvent for cellulose. After systematical research, we discovered a choline hydroxide/urea (ChOH/Ur) DES system as a sound direct solvent for cellulose. The degradation of cellulose during dissolution and regener- ation procedures is limited. The ChOH/Ur DES is prepared from widely used chemicals and can be used near room temp- erature, from 30–70 °C, which offers to save the system cost and energy. ChOH is primarily used to produce choline salts, a kind of food nutrient additive and safe enough to be used in baby food. ChOH itself is also widely used as the cleaning and degreasing agent in the metal industry. Urea is a biological metabolite and used as fertilizer. ChOH/Ur shows the advan- tages of high water tolerance and excellent recyclability. Our results suggest that ChOH/Ur system is a promising cheap solvent for cellulose, which could be developed into a state-of- the-art environmentally friendly platform for preparing regen- erated cellulose materials and a medium for cellulose chemistry. ## Experimental ### Materials Choline chloride (ChCl; 99%, Adamas-Beta) was recrystallized from absolute ethanol and vacuum dried at 50 °C overnight before use. The results confirm that cellulose degradation in the ChOH/Ur DES system is limited, and the ChOH/Ur solvent system is promising for preparing high-performance regener- ated cellulose materials. # Conclusions A systematic investigation has confirmed that almost all the ChCl-based DESs reported in the literature cannot dissolve cellulose. A new ChOH/Ur DES, with ChOH as the HBA and urea as HBD, was found with a sound solubility of cellulose. The ChOH/Ur system with ca. 11 wt% water can dissolve at least ~9.5 wt% cellulose with DP of 926 (cotton litter pulp). The maximum value of solubility was achieved at 70 °C within 30 min at the laboratory level. Our results also showed that the ChOH/Ur DES is tolerant to water. ChOH/Ur is a direct solvent system for cellulose, and no derivatizing reaction was found during the dissolution. Kamlet-Taft parameters of the EDSs were measured, and the results indicated that ChOH/Ur has a strong hydrogen bond basicity with the \u03b2 value of 1.88. The preliminary rheological results suggest that the dynamics of cellulose solution in ChOH/Ur system is similar to that of salt-free polyelectrolyte solutions. The degradation of cellulose during the dissolution and storage is limited. After the cellulose/ChOH/Ur solution was stored at 40 °C for 7 days, the DP of the regenerated cellulose remained about 80% of raw materials. The ChOH/Ur DES is recyclable without losing the solubility of cellulose. The ChOH/Ur DES is a promising solvent platform for preparing regenerated cellulose materials and may also be a media for cellulose chemistry. ## Conflicts of interest There are no conflicts to declare.
